NEW YORK (CNN) -- Olympic gold medalist Michael Phelps has acknowledged he engaged in "regrettable" behavior and "demonstrated bad judgment," after a British newspaper published a photograph of the swimmer smoking from a bong. Sports attorney Ryan Smith thinks Michael Phelps should speak to public about his opposition to drug use. Ryan Smith, a sports attorney and BET talk show host, on Monday spoke to John Roberts on CNN's "American Morning" about how the incident could affect Phelps' career. John Roberts: What was your reaction to news of this picture of Michael Phelps surfacing? Ryan Smith: The thing with Michael Phelps is, he's not only been an outspoken athlete against drugs so he's done a lot of testing, he's been supportive of WADA, which is the World Anti-Doping Agency. But he's really a guy of high character. So you look at this, and my first thought was, "What about his endorsement deals? What's going to happen in those?" A lot of endorsement deals have clauses that say that you can't do bad actions like this, not only crimes, but just things that you do bad in public could result in the termination of your contract. So he could lose a lot of money on this. Roberts: Now he never really admitted to smoking marijuana. ... The United States Olympic Committee isn't going to sanction him, it looks like, but did call his actions disappointing. But to the greater issue that you were talking about, in terms of his endorsement deals, do you think anybody is going to say, well, this is the straw that broke the camel's back with this guy? He had one incident back in 2004. But are you going to dump Michael Phelps because of this picture? Smith: It could happen, and the reason why is because a lot of these companies that are sponsoring him really are focused on kids and how actions of their athletes affect children. So that can be a big problem. The other thing is, unlike an athlete that plays sports every year in the public spotlight, the Olympics for swimmers comes only every four years. So he doesn't have that chance to rehabilitate his image immediately like a lot of other athletes, a basketball player or a football player would. So companies might say, you know what, let's not work with Michael Phelps right now, because he doesn't really have a chance to redeem himself. A picture says a thousand words, and how can he fight that? Roberts: How could you turn this around? If you were his attorney, if you were advising him what would you do? Smith: The first thing I would suggest is a drug test. And I know that that's not required. And I also know that he's not really going to have a problem with swimming in 2012. But I would just show that hey, I'm clean, I'm doing great. The next thing I would do is go out there in the public and talk about the troubles with working with drugs and really show the public that you are not about drug use, you are not about doing bad things in public. You are only about supporting the rules of WADA, the World Anti-Doping Agency, and supporting their drug testing program. So you can show that, hey, this is a minor incident, not a big deal. And really what it's all about is remaining clean. Roberts: If you were to lay a bet, would you say anybody drops him? Smith: I would say he'll have some problems. I don't know if I would say that a big sponsor would drop him, but I would say that a more wholesome-oriented sponsor might.

Below is an transcript excerpt from CNN’s *American Morning* broadcast in early February 2009, featuring host Kiran Chetry and HLN/CNN legal analyst Ryan Smith discussing the legal implications of the Michael Phelps bong photograph and the investigation launched by Richland County (South Carolina) Sheriff Leon Lott.

***

### **CNN AMERICAN MORNING**
**Date:** February 5, 2009  
**Topic:** Michael Phelps Bong Photo and Potential Criminal Charges  
**Hosts:** Kiran Chetry, John Roberts  
**Guest:** Ryan Smith (HLN Legal Analyst)

---

**KIRAN CHETRY (CNN HOST):** Welcome back to *American Morning*. We are following the fallout from that photograph showing Olympic hero Michael Phelps apparently smoking marijuana from a glass pipe at a party in South Carolina. 

Now, Phelps has already issued a public apology, and major sponsors like Speedo and Subway are standing by him. But now he could be facing legal trouble. The sheriff in Richland County, South Carolina, Leon Lott, says he is considering bringing criminal charges against Phelps. 

Joining us now to break down the legalities of all this is HLN legal analyst Ryan Smith. Ryan, good morning. 

**RYAN SMITH (LEGAL ANALYST):** Good morning, Kiran.

**CHETRY:** So Sheriff Leon Lott says no one is above the law in his county, and he wants to investigate this. But legally speaking, can you actually prosecute someone for drug possession based solely on a photograph published in a newspaper?

**RYAN SMITH:** It is an uphill battle for prosecutors, Kiran. It is very, very difficult. In criminal law, you generally need physical evidence—what we call the *corpus delicti*, the body of the crime. You need the actual substance to test it and prove beyond a reasonable doubt that it was, in fact, marijuana. 

A photograph doesn't tell you what was inside that pipe. Was it marijuana? Was it tobacco? Was it a legal herb? Was the pipe even real? A photograph alone usually isn't enough to secure a conviction in a court of law without supporting physical evidence or direct testimony from witnesses who were there.

**CHETRY:** So what would Sheriff Lott need to actually bring charges that stick?

**SMITH:** He would need people who were at that party to come forward and testify under oath. He’d need someone to say, "I was standing right next to him, I smelled marijuana, I handed him the pipe, and I know for a fact it was marijuana." 

Even then, without the actual physical drug present, any defense attorney worth their salt is going to question the credibility of witnesses—especially if those witnesses are potentially trying to get out of trouble themselves or looking for attention. 

**CHETRY:** Michael Phelps did issue an apology acknowledging "bad judgment." Does an apology like that count as a confession in a legal sense?

**SMITH:** That's a great question, but no. His statement was carefully crafted by a PR and legal team. He apologized for "inappropriate behavior" and "bad judgment." He never explicitly stated, "I was smoking illegal marijuana on that night in South Carolina." 

So legally, that statement is not an admission of a crime. It’s an admission of a PR disaster, but it falls way short of a legal confession that a prosecutor could use in court.

**CHETRY:** What about the rumor that the person who took the photo was trying to sell it for $100,000? Could extortion charges come into play here?

**SMITH:** Absolutely. If someone approached Phelps's team and said, "Pay me money or I’m going to publish this photograph," that crosses the line into extortion or blackmail. So while Sheriff Lott is looking at Phelps, federal or local authorities could potentially look at whoever took and distributed the photo if money was demanded to keep it quiet.

**CHETRY:** So bottom line, Ryan—do you think Michael Phelps actually ends up in a courtroom over this?

**SMITH:** Highly unlikely. Unless someone hands the police the actual pipe with Phelps's fingerprints and traceable marijuana residue on it, this investigation will likely end without formal charges. Sheriff Lott is making a point that famous athletes aren't above the law, but from a strictly legal standpoint, the evidence just isn't there right now.

**CHETRY:** Ryan Smith, HLN legal analyst, thanks so much for joining us this morning.

**SMITH:** Thanks, Kiran.

***

### **Context & Aftermath:**
* **Outcome:** Shortly after this coverage, Sheriff Leon Lott officially announced on February 16, 2009, that no charges would be filed against Michael Phelps due to a lack of physical evidence, confirming the legal analysis provided during the broadcast.
* **Sponsor Reaction:** While Subway, Speedo, and Omega retained Phelps, Kellogg's decided not to renew his endorsement contract when it expired.

**BALTIMORE, Md.** — A picture may be worth a thousand words, but for Olympic superstar Michael Phelps, a single photograph published over the weekend could cost millions of dollars. 

Just six months after making history in Beijing by winning an unprecedented eight gold medals, the 23-year-old swimming icon finds himself embroiled in a major public relations crisis. The fallout comes after the British tabloid *News of the World* published a photo appearing to show Phelps smoking marijuana from a glass pipe at a college party in South Carolina. 

Phelps issued a swift apology on Sunday, acknowledging he engaged in "regrettable" behavior and demonstrated "bad judgment." However, the public admission has left his lucrative endorsement portfolio—estimated at over $10 million annually—hanging in the balance. Major global brands including Speedo, Visa, Subway, and Kellogg’s are now forced to weigh their association with the world's most decorated swimmer against the potential damage to their corporate images.

As the sports world reacts, legal experts and brand strategists are debating whether this misstep will result in a temporary slap on the wrist or the catastrophic collapse of "Brand Phelps."

***

### **TRANSCRIPT: CNN AMERICAN MORNING**

**DATE:** February 2, 2009  
**ANCHOR:** John Roberts  
**GUEST:** Ryan Smith (Sports Attorney and Legal Analyst)

---

**JOHN ROBERTS:** Welcome back. He is the most decorated Olympian of all time, a American hero who captured the world's imagination in Beijing. But today, Michael Phelps is treaded in deep water off the pool. A photograph published over the weekend showing Phelps using a marijuana pipe has sparked a media frenzy and left his corporate sponsors in a very difficult position. 

Joining us now to break down the legal and financial ramifications is sports attorney Ryan Smith. Ryan, good morning to you.

**RYAN SMITH:** Good morning, John.

**ROBERTS:** Ryan, let’s get right to the bottom line here. Michael Phelps has multi-million-dollar deals with companies like Kellogg’s, Speedo, Subway, and Visa. How much financial jeopardy is he actually in right now?

**SMITH:** He’s in significant financial jeopardy, John. Virtually every major endorsement contract for an athlete of Phelps' caliber contains what we call a "morals clause." These clauses give corporations the right to unilaterally terminate a contract or suspend payments if the athlete engages in behavior that brings public disrepute, contempt, or scandal to themselves, or by extension, to the brand. Smoking marijuana—an illegal substance under state and federal law—is a textbook trigger for a morals clause.

**ROBERTS:** So the legal mechanism is there for these companies to walk away. But do you expect them to actually drop him? Or does his status as an eight-time gold medalist give him a pass?

**SMITH:** It really depends on the brand's target demographic. You’re going to see a split strategy here, John. For a company like Kellogg’s, which markets directly to families and young children, a photo of an Olympic hero smoking out of a bong is toxic. I would not be surprised if family-centric brands cut ties or allow his contracts to quietly expire. On the other hand, brands like Speedo or Subway, which cater to a broader or slightly older demographic, may take a "wait-and-see" approach. Speedo has already issued a statement calling his behavior a personal mistake, but they haven't dropped him yet. They know that in three years, London 2012 is coming, and Phelps is still the fastest man in the water.

**ROBERTS:** Phelps issued an apology very quickly, saying he used "bad judgment" and promised his fans it wouldn't happen again. From a crisis management standpoint, did his legal and PR team handle this correctly?

**SMITH:** Absolutely. The worst thing he could have done was deny the authenticity of the photo or try to lie about it, especially in the digital age where more photos or videos could surface. By admitting it immediately, expressing regret, and falling on his sword, he effectively ended the "whodunit" phase of the news cycle. However, the legal exposure isn't completely gone. 

**ROBERTS:** Let's talk about that legal exposure. Could he actually face criminal charges in South Carolina where the photo was allegedly taken?

**SMITH:** Technically, yes, but practically, it's very unlikely. Local law enforcement in Richland County, South Carolina, could theoretically investigate, but prosecuting someone based solely on a photograph without the actual physical evidence—meaning the marijuana itself—is a massive uphill battle for any prosecutor. The bigger immediate threat to Phelps isn't the police; it's USA Swimming and the International Olympic Committee. 

**ROBERTS:** Meaning a suspension from competition?

**SMITH:** Exactly. Even though this didn't occur during competition and isn't a performance-enhancing drug case under WADA [World Anti-Doping Agency] rules out-of-competition, governing bodies have code-of-conduct policies. USA Swimming could suspend him for a period of months, which would derail his training for the upcoming World Championships in Rome later this year.

**ROBERTS:** Ryan, big picture: Michael Phelps is 23 years old. He's young. Is "Brand Phelps" permanently damaged, or can he bounce back from this?

**SMITH:** In America, we love a comeback story almost as much as we love a champion. If Phelps stays clean, stays out of trouble, and dominates in London in 2012, this will be remembered as a minor bump in the road—a youthful mistake. But his margin for error is now zero. One more misstep, and the corporate money will dry up permanently.

**ROBERTS:** A zero-tolerance world for the golden boy. Ryan Smith, sports attorney, thanks so much for your insights this morning.

**SMITH:** Thanks for having me, John.

The scandal triggered intense media coverage. Reactions from legal and sports experts were nuanced, dividing along lines of law enforcement authority, athletic governance, and corporate crisis management.

---

### 1. Reactions from Legal Experts
The legal reaction focused largely on the actions of **Richland County Sheriff Leon Lott**, who launched a high-profile criminal investigation into Phelps, threatening to charge the swimmer with drug possession despite having only a photograph as evidence.

* **Critique of "Overzealous" Prosecution:** Legal experts overwhelmingly criticized Sheriff Lott’s investigation. Prominent criminal defense attorneys and legal commentators noted that a photograph alone is generally insufficient to prove illegal drug possession, as it cannot prove what substance was inside the pipe, nor can it establish physical possession of an illegal drug beyond a reasonable doubt.
* **Waste of Resources:** Former prosecutors appearing on legal panels argued that spending public resources to prosecute a high-profile athlete over a months-old photo set a dangerous precedent of selective prosecution driven by publicity. 
* **Outcome:** Under intense public and legal scrutiny—and lacking physical evidence or cooperative witnesses—Sheriff Lott dropped the investigation without filing charges against Phelps, though seven other people associated with the party were arrested.

---

### 2. Reactions from Sports Experts and Governing Bodies
Sports analysts and athletic authorities focused on two main elements: whether the act constituted a performance-enhancing violation, and Phelps's status as a role model.

* **World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) & IOC:** The International Olympic Committee (IOC) and WADA noted that marijuana was only banned **in-competition**. Because the incident occurred during Phelps's off-season, it was not an anti-doping violation. The IOC accepted his public apology and praised him for his "mature" response.
* **USA Swimming:** USA Swimming took a tougher stance to protect the sport’s image, suspending Phelps from competition for three months and withdrawing its financial support during that period. They stated: *"This is not a situation where any anti-doping rule was violated, but we decided to send a strong message to Michael because he disappointed so many people."*
* **Sports Analysts:** Commentators (such as those on ESPN and NBC) were split. Some argued the controversy was overblown because marijuana is not a performance-enhancing drug (PED) and Phelps was a 23-year-old taking a break after an unprecedented athletic achievement. Others argued that his immense status came with a responsibility to youth, and that his lapse in judgment damaged his reputation.

---

But other sponsors, like Subway and Speedo, are standing by him. 
> 
> Joining me now from Los Angeles is crisis PR expert Howard Bragman. Howard, Kellogg says goodbye, but Subway says hello. Why the split among these big brands?
> 
> **HOWARD BRAGMAN (CRISIS PR EXPERT):** Well, Kyra, you have to look at who these brands sell to. Kellogg's sells Frosted Flakes and Pop-Tarts to moms with young kids. They operate in a zero-tolerance world for family values. They didn't want to deal with angry parents at the grocery store. 
> 
> On the other hand, brands like Speedo, Subway, and Under Armour target young adults, sports fans, and a demographic that is much more forgiving of a 23-year-old making a mistake at a college party.
> 
> **PHILLIPS:** Right, and Phelps issued a pretty quick apology. He called it "bad judgment" and promised it wouldn't happen again. From a public relations standpoint, did he handle this the right way out of the gate?
> 
> **BRAGMAN:** Absolutely. Rule number one in crisis management: Own it, apologize, and do it fast. He didn't say, "That's not me," or "It was tobacco." He admitted he made a mistake, he took responsibility, and he apologized to his fans and his family. That cuts off the speculation. You can't investigate someone who has already confessed.
> 
> **PHILLIPS:** So what are the next steps for Michael Phelps to rebuild his brand and save the rest of his endorsements?
> 
> **BRAGMAN:** It’s a three-step recovery plan:
> 
> First, **lay low.** Get off the party circuit, stop going to clubs, and get back into the pool. The public wants to see him doing what he does best, which is swimming. 
> 
> Second, **do the work quietly.** Don't do a massive PR apology tour on late-night TV right now. Show contrition through actions, not soundbites.
> 
> Third, **let time and performance heal the wound.** American audiences love a redemption story. If Michael gets back in the gym, qualifies for the World Championships, and breaks more records, by the time London 2012 rolls around, this bong photo will just be a minor footnote in an incredible career.
> 
> **PHILLIPS:** Howard Bragman, crisis PR expert. Howard, thanks for your time today.
> 
> **BRAGMAN:** Thank you, Kyra.

***

### Outcome of the Strategy
The PR strategy outlined above proved highly effective:

**NETWORK SPORTS SPECIAL REPORT**
**DATE:** February 6, 2009  
**SUBJECT:** Michael Phelps Photo Controversy: Legal and Corporate Fallout  

---

### **[NEWS REPORT]**

**ANCHOR (Studio):** 
Good evening. Tonight, the fallout continues for 14-time Olympic gold medalist Michael Phelps following the publication of a sensational photograph showing the swimming superstar using a glass pipe at a college party. 

The image, published last Sunday by the British tabloid *News of the World*, was reportedly taken at the University of South Carolina in November—just months after Phelps made history by winning eight gold medals at the Beijing Olympics. 

Phelps issued a swift public apology, acknowledging "bad judgment" and promising his fans and sponsors it would not happen again. However, the repercussions have been immediate. USA Swimming has handed down a three-month suspension from competition, cutting off financial support during that window. 

In the corporate world, the reaction has been mixed. While long-time swimsuit sponsor Speedo and watchmaker Omega have announced they will stand by the swimmer, cereal giant Kellogg’s announced yesterday that it will not renew its endorsement contract with Phelps, stating his behavior is "not consistent with the image of Kellogg."

To break down the complex legal landscape surrounding athlete endorsements, morality clauses, and anti-doping regulations, we are joined by prominent sports attorney Ryan Smith.

---

### **[INTERVIEW SNIPPET]**

**ANCHOR:** 
Ryan, thank you for being with us. Let’s start with the corporate side of this. Kellogg’s dropped him almost immediately, while Speedo is sticking by his side. From a legal standpoint, how do these endorsement contracts allow a company to walk away so quickly after a single incident?

**RYAN SMITH:** 
Thanks for having me. What we’re seeing unfold right now is a textbook execution of what we call a "Morality Clause" or a "Termination for Cause" provision. Virtually every high-profile endorsement contract contains language that allows a brand to unilaterally sever ties if an athlete engages in behavior that brings public disrepute, contempt, or scandal upon themselves, or by extension, the brand. 

The threshold for triggering these clauses is intentionally broad. A brand like Kellogg’s—which targets families and young children—has a very low tolerance for any implication of illegal drug use. They don't need a criminal conviction; the mere existence of the photo and Phelps's admission of guilt is legally sufficient for them to activate that exit clause without facing a breach-of-contract lawsuit from Phelps's legal team.

**ANCHOR:** 
And what about brands like Speedo or Subway who chose to stay? Are their contracts written differently?

**RYAN SMITH:** 
The language in the contracts is likely very similar, but the business calculation is different. Speedo’s brand identity is intrinsically linked to pure athletic performance, and Phelps is the greatest swimmer in history. For Kellogg's, he was a spokesperson for breakfast cereal. Legally, both companies had the option to terminate under the morality clause. It comes down to corporate risk tolerance and brand alignment, not a difference in legal leverage.

**ANCHOR:** 
Let's turn to the athletic regulations. A lot of fans are asking why USA Swimming suspended him for three months, but anti-doping agencies like USADA or WADA haven't issued a multi-year ban. Why isn't this considered a anti-doping violation?

**RYAN SMITH:** 
This is a critical legal distinction that often gets lost in the headlines. Under the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) Code, cannabis is classified as a "specified substance," but crucially, it is only prohibited **in-competition**. 

Because this photograph was taken in November—during Phelps's off-season, months away from any official sanctioned competition—he was not subject to in-competition testing rules for recreational drugs. If USADA had tested him at that party and found THC in his system, under the rules at the time, it still wouldn't constitute a Doping Rule Violation because it occurred out-of-competition. 

**ANCHOR:** 
So USA Swimming's suspension isn't an anti-doping penalty at all?

**RYAN SMITH:** 
Not at all. USA Swimming suspended him under their Code of Conduct rules regarding the "best interests of the sport" and maintaining the integrity of the organization. It’s a governing body disciplinary action, not a WADA anti-doping sanction. From a legal perspective, Phelps hasn't violated anti-doping law; he violated his governing body’s code of conduct and the trust of his corporate sponsors.

**ANCHOR:** 
Ryan Smith, sports attorney and legal analyst, thanks for clearing that up for us.

**RYAN SMITH:** 
My pleasure.
